newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-CHESTERFIELD READY TO CLAIM PLACE IN HISTORY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CHESTERFIELD READY TO CLAIM PLACE IN HISTORY.

text.p: Chelsea, Middlesbrough and Wimbledon have upset the real giants of English soccer to reach this weekend's F.A. Cup semifinals.
But they could find their achievements completely overshadowed by a little-known fourth contender for the cup -- Chesterfield.
The second division club have surprised everyone, including themselves, by reaching the last four of the world's oldest domestic cup competition.
Victory over Middlesbrough at Old Trafford on Sunday would assure them of a truly astonishing place in the final.

This is the first time the Spireites, who take their nickname from their town's famous crooked church spire, have reached the final four of the cup and their success says much for the abilities of manager John Duncan, a former striker with Tottenham Hotspur and Derby County.
The club's previous best cup runs were in 1933, 1938 and 1950, when on each occasion they reached the fifth round.
That is a poor record considering they are the fourth oldest club in the Football League.
"Our cup record in the past has been fairly dismal but now we can make up for all those disappointments," club captain Sean Dyche acknowledged.
Chesterfield were formed in 1866, but it was 1899 before they were elected to the second division.
At the time, their only claim to fame was an eccentric taste in team kit. In the 1890-91 season they played in Union Jack shirts.
After losing their league status in 1909, the Derbyshire club were re-admitted in 1921, when division three north was formed, and they moved up to the second division in 1931.
In the following two decades, the club moved between the second and third division, winning promotion from the third in 1931 and 1936 and being relegated in 1933 and 1951.
Since then, the club have been consigned to the bottom two divisions of the English league. Their only major success before this season was their record of producing top-class goalkeepers.
Former England keepers Sam Hardy and Gordon Banks both played for Chesterfield, as did highly-regarded keepers Steve Orgrizovic, John Osborne and Alan Stevenson.

For captain Dyche, who helped his side to victories over Bury, Scarborough, Bristol City, Bolton, Nottingham Forest and Wrexham in this season's cup run, this weekend provides a great chance to rewrite the history books.
The former Nottingham Forest utility player, who arrived at Chesterfield on a free transfer, has made more than 200 appearances for the Saltergate club and is confident they can win.

"The thing with the cup is that it is only over 90 minutes," he said. "And just to play a premier league team does not mean they are naturally going to win. If they do then so be it, but if they don't then it is a great result for us. The pressure is on them.

"Everybody will say they should win because they have players that are used to big occasions. But if they lose, everybody will talk about a giant-killing. The only pressure on us is the pressure we put on ourselves.
"There is no sort of exact secret in us beating those sides but just hard work and determination and the will to win," he said.
"The manager sets us up tactically on how he thinks we should play. Then we get on with our individual jobs."
